Chapter 8: The Business of Death and Renewal
Running a trauma cleaning business means stepping into a world most folks would rather avoid. It's not just about scrubbing floors or changing sheets—there are practical hurdles, like finding clients, managing a team, and wading through a mountain of paperwork and regulations. But honestly, there’s something even tougher: convincing people that this work really matters, and that it deserves respect.
Sandra never planned on owning a business. It all started out of necessity—a way to make ends meet when other doors had closed. Those first jobs trickled in: a social worker’s referral here, a frantic landlord’s call there. But word started to spread. Before long, Sandra’s phone was ringing a lot more, each call a new request for help. What began as a last resort quickly became a lifeline—not just for Sandra, but for her whole team, and the clients who needed them.
Of course, there were days when it all felt like too much. Sometimes the phone wouldn’t stop ringing, each call bringing news of another tragedy, another home that needed their care. Sandra and her team would load up the van—protective suits, masks, heavy-duty cleaners—and set out, never quite knowing what they’d find on the other side of the door. Every job was different, a new puzzle that demanded both creativity and grit. Some days, the work was fairly straightforward; other times, it took days just to make a home livable again.
The business brought Sandra into contact with all sorts of people—police officers, social workers, grieving families, landlords, tenants. She learned to navigate the red tape of death and loss, filling out endless forms, negotiating with officials, and standing up for clients who had no one else in their corner. It became clear that trauma cleaning wasn’t just about cleaning up physical messes—it was about helping people through some of the most difficult moments of their lives.
There were moments Sandra felt proud—like when a client called just to say thank you, or when a team member managed to overcome their own struggles, or when a home was transformed from a place of sadness to a place of hope. But there were also tough days. Payments came in late. Sometimes jobs fell through. And there was always that lingering stigma, making it hard for people to see the value in what Sandra’s team did. So, she learned to celebrate the small wins, to find meaning in the daily grind.
Over time, this business turned into something much bigger than just a job—it became a mission. Sandra saw how much her work mattered, how it gave people a fresh start and a chance to move forward. In a world obsessed with keeping up appearances, there’s something truly radical about caring for the messes everyone else wants to ignore.
The business of death and renewal, at its core, is really about hope. It’s about offering people the chance to begin again—even when that seems impossible.
